analysis.one_liner: Caps rent-to- store fees and interest at state retail-sale limits and requires full price disclosure.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the Senate in September 2006 and referred to the Banking Committee, where it died without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: Rent-to-own stores let customers take home furniture, appliances, and electronics with weekly payments and an option to own the item eventually. Because these contracts are legally leases rather than loans, customers often miss out on the price caps, disclosure rules, and debt-collection protections that apply to regular credit sales, and the total cost can far exceed the item's cash price. This bill would have applied those same state fee caps and federal lending and collection laws to rent-to-own deals, required stores to show the cash price, annual percentage rate, and total of payments on each item's tag and contract, and let customers sue stores that broke the rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Rent-to-own customers, who are disproportionately low-income and live in minority neighborhoods, would see the total cost of acquiring goods capped at what state law allows for regular installment sales, get clear written disclosure of the true cost, and gain the right to sue with statutory damages and attorney fees if a store hides costs or harasses them.

how_it_helps.text: The bill bars rent-to-own sellers from charging any interest, fees, or finance charges beyond what state law permits on a comparable retail installment sale, closing the gap that lets rent-to-own contracts cost more than the same purchase financed through a store credit sale [S2] [S3].

It requires tags and contracts to show the cash price, the annual percentage rate, the payment amount and number of payments, and the total of payments needed to own the item, so customers can compare the rent-to-own deal to simply buying the item [S2] [S3].

It extends the Truth in Lending Act, Equal Credit Opportunity Act, Fair Debt Collection Practices Act, and Fair Credit Reporting Act to rent-to-own transactions, and bans threatening criminal prosecution, harassment, and deceptive collection practices [S2] [S3].

Customers could sue for actual damages plus $250 per disclosure failure or $2,500 per other violation, with attorney fees and costs awarded, and the Federal Trade Commission could enforce the rules [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Rent-to-own dealers would bear the cost: their fees and finance charges would be capped at state retail-installment limits, their collection practices would face federal restrictions, and they would face statutory damages and FTC enforcement for violations. Customers who rely on immediate access to goods without credit checks could see fewer stores or higher upfront prices as the industry's pricing model tightened.

drawbacks.text: The bill preserves the rent-to-own model itself, including the customer's right to cancel at any time; it caps excess fees but does not make rent-to-own cheaper than saving up or using regular credit, so customers could still pay more overall than a cash buyer [S3].

A cap of $100 on termination fees (5 percent of cash price) and recovery fees for unreturned goods would still be added on top of permitted finance charges, and honest supporters would acknowledge that some customers who depend on no-credit-check access could face tighter store terms or fewer locations if the pricing model became unprofitable [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the people who use rent-to-own stores, the disclosure, fee-cap, and collection protections would directly address the problem the bill itself identifies: customers who intend to own the goods often pay far more than the cash price without knowing it. The main cost falls on the rent-to-own industry's profit margins rather than on customers, though the bill leaves the underlying lease model intact and does not guarantee anyone credit they cannot get elsewhere.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Banking Committee in late September 2006 and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Sen. Charles Schumer introduced the Rent-To-Own Reform Act of 2006 in the Senate on September 29, 2006 [S1] [S5].
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs; no further action appears in the record for the remainder of the 109th Congress [S5].

The bill's own findings stated that the rent-to-own industry targets its products primarily to low-income and minority neighborhoods and that dealers often fail to disclose key terms, engage in unfair collection practices, and charge excessive fees and rates [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Rent-to-own dealers, who could keep charging fees and effective rates above what state law allows for comparable installment sales, without the disclosure and collection restrictions the bill would have imposed.

for.name: Sen. Charles E. Schumer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its sole sponsor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day of introduction and took no further action on it before the Congress ended.

against.name: Richard Shelby
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup.

sides.party_line_note: Only one senator, a Democrat, sponsored the bill and no one cosponsored or voted on it, so no partisan pattern was ever visible.

industries.note: The bill would cap the fees and finance charges these dealers may assess at the levels state law allows for comparable retail installment sales, and would subject their collections practices to federal debt-collection law and FTC enforcement [S3]. The industry's business depends on charging more over the life of a contract than the item's cash price, aimed at customers who lack credit access; its gain comes at those customers' expense [S3].
